/reaction-test.title: Reaction Time Test
/reaction-test.subtitle: Measure visual reaction time in the browser with PULSE.

sections.heading: What is reaction time?
paragraphs: Reaction time is the interval between a stimulus being presented and the start of a response. A result is influenced by stimulus processing, decision-making, and the physical action used to respond.

sections.heading: How the PULSE test works
paragraphs: PULSE runs 10 visual reaction trials. Each trial uses a randomized foreperiod between 100ms and 3000ms, with short and long preparation intervals, to reduce anticipatory guessing. The visual stimulus appears after the delay, and you respond with the spacebar or a touch input.

sections.heading: How results are measured
paragraphs: PULSE records monotonic millisecond timestamps from stimulus presentation to the detected input event. An estimated display refresh adjustment is applied using the detected frame interval. This is a mathematical model of display timing, not a physical hardware sensor measurement.

sections.heading: Factors that influence results
paragraphs: Reaction-time results can vary with sleep, fatigue, caffeine, time of day, attention, distraction, and posture. Repeating the test under similar conditions makes comparisons more useful.

sections.heading: Hardware and device differences
paragraphs: Display refresh rate, input-device polling rate, wireless transmission, browser rendering, and other local hardware factors can add latency. A higher refresh rate can reduce the interval between display refresh opportunities, while peripheral polling rates can change how quickly an input is reported. PULSE estimates display-frame timing but cannot measure or remove every local hardware delay.

sections.heading: How to test consistently
paragraphs: For repeat measurements, use the same device and input method when possible. Keep the testing environment similar and close demanding background tasks that could interrupt browser performance.

sections.heading: Understanding your result
paragraphs: PULSE reports average and median response times along with consistency and false-start information. Responses below 80ms are treated as false starts because they are unlikely to represent a normal visual reaction and can indicate anticipation.

sections.heading: Browser testing limitations
paragraphs: Browser timing APIs can provide fine-grained timestamps, but timestamp resolution is different from end-to-end physical measurement accuracy. A browser reaction test should be treated as a benchmark of performance under a given setup, not as a laboratory measurement or a medical or neurological diagnostic.

faq.question: Why can my reaction-time score change between devices?
faq.answer: Different displays, input devices, browser workloads, and operating-system paths can introduce different amounts of latency. Use the same setup when comparing repeated results.

faq.question: Can I improve my reaction-time score by practicing?
faq.answer: Practice can make you more familiar with the task and its response method. That can change performance, so keep practice history in mind when comparing results.

faq.question: Why are responses under 80ms false starts?
faq.answer: PULSE treats responses below 80ms as anticipatory responses rather than normal visual reaction times.

/direction-test.title: Directional Choice Test: Response Speed
/direction-test.subtitle: Measure directional choice reaction time and accuracy with PULSE.

sections.heading: What is choice reaction time?
paragraphs: Choice reaction time includes both recognizing which stimulus is present and selecting the matching motor response. It adds a decision component to a simple single-response reaction task.

sections.heading: How the test works
paragraphs: PULSE presents an arrow pointing up, down, left, or right. There are 10 trials, with a randomized delay between 1000ms and 3000ms. You respond with the corresponding arrow key or the on-screen direction control.

sections.heading: Scoring and speed-accuracy balance
paragraphs: PULSE records response time for correct trials and reports accuracy across the assessment. Looking at both speed and accuracy helps distinguish a fast response from a fast response that frequently selects the wrong direction.

sections.heading: Performance factors and limitations
paragraphs: Keyboard ergonomics, switch travel, display latency, visual search, and how quickly you discriminate the four directions can affect results. Browser timing measures the response path available to the application and does not remove every source of hardware or operating-system latency.

faq.question: How is this different from a simple reaction-time test?
faq.answer: A simple reaction task can use one response to one stimulus. The directional task requires you to identify one of several possible directions and choose the matching response.

faq.question: Why are accurate responses important for the score?
faq.answer: A response-time result is more useful when the response is also correct. PULSE reports accuracy alongside response speed.

/colour-recognition.title: Colour Recognition Test: Stroop Task
/colour-recognition.subtitle: Test selective attention and response speed with PULSE's colour recognition assessment.

sections.heading: What the task measures
paragraphs: The task introduces cognitive conflict by asking you to respond either to a written colour word or to the ink colour used to display it. This kind of conflict is commonly discussed in relation to the Stroop effect.

sections.heading: How the test works
paragraphs: PULSE runs 15 rounds that alternate between matching the written word and matching the displayed ink colour. The available colour buttons are shuffled so their positions change between rounds.

sections.heading: Scoring and interference
paragraphs: Results include response time and accuracy. PULSE also calculates an interference measure from the latency difference between conflicting and matching rounds.

sections.heading: Viewing factors and limitations
paragraphs: Display brightness, contrast, viewing conditions, and the visual search required to locate a shuffled response button can affect performance. This assessment is a cognitive benchmark and is not a clinical colour-vision or colour-blindness test.

faq.question: Why do the colour buttons move between rounds?
faq.answer: The buttons are shuffled between rounds so a user cannot rely on a fixed button position instead of identifying the required colour response.

faq.question: What is the Stroop effect?
faq.answer: It describes the response conflict that can occur when an automatic reading response competes with the task of naming an ink colour.

/block-memory.title: Block Memory Test: Spatial Sequence Recall
/block-memory.subtitle: Test visual and spatial sequence recall with a 3x3 block grid.

sections.heading: What is spatial working memory?
paragraphs: Spatial working memory involves briefly retaining the locations of visual information and recalling them in sequence. PULSE uses a small grid to make the task concrete and repeatable.

sections.heading: How the test works
paragraphs: PULSE uses a 3x3 grid. Sequences start at length 2, and each block is highlighted for 400ms with a 200ms pause. You then tap the blocks in the same order. The assessment provides three lives.

sections.heading: Progression and scoring
paragraphs: A correct sequence advances the level and produces a longer sequence. Incorrect responses consume a life. The result records the highest level and longest sequence recalled along with overall accuracy and total time.

sections.heading: Factors and limitations
paragraphs: Visual grouping strategies, attention, and the accuracy of touch input can influence results. PULSE is an educational benchmark and is not a clinical memory evaluation.

faq.question: How do the sequence lengths increase?
faq.answer: The sequence begins at length 2 and increases by one block as you successfully complete levels.

faq.question: What happens when I make a mistake?
faq.answer: An incorrect sequence consumes a life. The test continues while lives remain and ends when all lives are used.

/number-memory.title: Number Memory Test: Forward Digit Recall
/number-memory.subtitle: Measure forward digit recall and working-memory span with PULSE.

sections.heading: What is digit span memory?
paragraphs: Digit span is a short-term memory task in which you briefly retain a sequence of numbers and reproduce it. PULSE uses forward recall, so the digits are entered in the same order in which they were shown.

sections.heading: How the test works
paragraphs: PULSE starts at 3 digits. Display time scales with sequence length using a minimum of 1000ms and an additional 500ms per digit. After the sequence disappears, you enter it using the keypad or keyboard. The assessment provides three lives.

sections.heading: Progression and scoring
paragraphs: A correct entry increases the digit count by one. An incorrect entry consumes a life. The final result records the highest level reached, longest sequence, accuracy, correct attempts, and total time.

sections.heading: Strategies and limitations
paragraphs: Chunking digits into small groups can make a sequence easier to rehearse. Typing speed and the response method can also affect the task. PULSE is a benchmark of the implemented memory task, not an IQ test or a clinical diagnostic tool.

faq.question: How long are the digits shown?
faq.answer: Display time is scaled to sequence length with a minimum of 1000ms plus 500ms for each digit.

faq.question: Does the number have to be entered in the same order?
faq.answer: Yes. PULSE measures forward digit recall, so the sequence must be entered in the original order.
